goal: Help an engineering team choose between RAG, fine-tuning, and a hybrid approach for enterprise AI assistants by comparing data freshness, evaluation, latency, cost, and security while preserving evidence limits and avoiding unsupported rankings.
reader_objective: Give an engineering team a dimension-by-dimension comparison of RAG, fine-tuning, and hybrid architectures for enterprise AI assistants — covering data freshness, evaluation, latency, cost, and security — with the strength and disagreements of the underlying evidence made explicit so the team can run its own decision rather than adopt a vendor's ranking.
evidence_types: vendor and product blog guidance (majority of sources)
independent academic systems research (arXiv study of RAG inference trade-offs)
security incident reporting and trade-press analysis (csoonline)
evaluation-methodology guidance with named metrics, benchmarks, and tooling
quantitative cost and latency estimates tied to specific provider pricing
adoption survey statistics and modeled cost curves
governance and access-control architecture reference material
limitations: Almost all sources are vendor or product content (superannotate, vectorize, codelamda, v2solutions, orq.ai, upstash, coreweave, Google Cloud, agicent, Databricks, actian, labelyourdata, montecarlo, nextgencoding, ai-de.net, Tencent, c3.unu.edu) with commercial incentives and self-referential 'best practice' framing.

Only one source is independent research (S-18, arXiv), and it characterizes RAG inference systems in isolation rather than comparing RAG against a fine-tuned baseline on a shared task; it also states its study 'is not exhaustive'.

No source reports a controlled head-to-head RAG-vs-fine-tuning experiment on the same enterprise workload; benchmark numbers cited (SWE-bench, BIRD-SQL, an agriculture benchmark, RAFT) come second-hand through vendor posts.

Cost and latency figures depend on specific model pricing and hardware rates (GPT-5.2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Pinecone, A10G/H100 rates) and on assumed token volumes, so they date quickly and are not directly comparable across sources.

Publication dates span 2024-04 to 2026-10; the older pieces (S-01, S-03, S-09, S-12) predate several referenced pricing and model changes, and S-23 is a forward-looking 2026-2030 projection with claims attributed to secondary citations rather than primary data.

Several sources assert a general winner (for example S-19's FAQ preference for RAG, S-06's preference for fine-tuning on coherence and latency), which conflicts with the goal's instruction to avoid unsupported rankings; these are recorded as source claims, not adopted.

Security evidence is split between RAG-side threat reporting (S-27) and access-control architecture (S-24); there is no comparable security analysis of fine-tuned model deployment beyond ACL and deletion limitations.
Evaluation evidence is heavily RAG-centric; fine-tuning evaluation appears only as short general guidance.
Some sources (S-26, S-23) are promotional or AI-generated-looking syntheses with dense unattributed statistics ('15-40% gains', '86% of organizations') that cannot be verified within the corpus.

findings.statement: RAG can refresh what a model knows at query time without retraining, whereas a fine-tuned model's knowledge is fixed to the data snapshot used in training and changing it requires another training cycle.

evidence.excerpt: Retrieval pipelines reflect new data as soon as it is indexed into knowledge bases—no retraining required.
Fine tuned models are limited by the exact snapshot of data at training time, and updates require gathering new data and running another training cycle.
A fine-tuned model remains limited to what it saw during its last training session.
All successful models require continuous fine-tuning to introduce new information and stay relevant. It’s a repeated process, not just a one-and-done.
evidence.context: Suggests fine-tuning is not a one-time act, which softens a simple 'set and forget' reading of the fine-tuning side

qualifications: The freshness advantage is about where knowledge lives, not about answer quality; several sources note RAG answers are only as current and correct as the indexed corpus.

findings.statement: Sources broadly converge that fine-tuning is the tool for changing model behavior — tone, style, and output format — while RAG is the tool for supplying changing knowledge.

evidence.excerpt: RAG is used primarily to inject new knowledge into a model, while fine tuning is best for changing behavior, tone, or task structure.
matching a domain writing style a prompt can't capture (legal drafting, clinical notes)
evidence.context: Listed among the three workflows the source says fine-tuning uniquely solves

evidence.excerpt: Fine-tuning is the way to teach a model about writing styles or output formats.
If you want to give a model specific instructions for a well-defined task, you might consider SFT, also often referred to as Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning (PEFT).
evidence.context: Google Cloud method survey placing supervised fine-tuning alongside RAG, RLHF, and distillation

findings.statement: RAG adds retrieval stages that increase time-to-first-token, tail latency, and end-to-end latency, while a fine-tuned model can answer without a retrieval hop — but the corpus cautions that the fine-tuning latency advantage is not guaranteed.

evidence.excerpt: Takeaway 1: Compared to baseline LLM inference, RAG-based LLMs introduce additional overheads that prolong TTFT inference latency.
evidence.context: Independent systems study; measured, not vendor guidance

evidence.excerpt: we find that naively re-retrieving can increase the end-to-end latency to nearly 30 seconds, precluding production deployment
RAG adds latency through vector search, re-ranking overhead, and extended transformer prefill phases.
A multi-step inference pipeline adds latency relative to direct fine tuned model calls.
A fine-tuned model may be larger or more complex than a retrieval-based alternative, which can impact**inference speed** , especially in production environments with latency constraints.
evidence.context: Directly contests the assumption that fine-tuning always wins on latency

qualifications: S-18 measures RAG pipelines against a baseline LLM, not against a fine-tuned model on the same task and hardware.
Latency depends on retrieval index choice, batching, reranking, and context length, so published millisecond figures are configuration-specific.

findings.statement: Fine-tuning concentrates cost at the start — data preparation, training compute, and experimentation — and can lower per-query input-token cost, which sources say pays off at high, stable volume.

evidence.excerpt: Fine-tuning concentrates cost at the beginning, while marginal cost per request remains relatively stable as traffic grows.
Fine tuning incurs high upfront training costs but can reduce per-inference costs by enabling smaller, specialized adapted models to replace large generalist systems.
For fixed-domain, high-throughput use cases, fine-tuning a small model yields an order-of-magnitude cost reduction over running long-context RAG prompts through public frontier APIs.
data preparation consumes 20 to 40 percent
evidence.context: Fine-tuning budget breakdown; data prep is the largest hidden line item

qualifications: Upfront figures range from under $20 of GPU time for one QLoRA run (S-20) to $1,000-$20,000 for a LoRA program (S-05), reflecting different model sizes and data-prep scope.
Costs assume the domain is stable enough that the training investment is amortized over many queries.

findings.statement: RAG has low setup cost but incurs recurring per-query retrieval and context-token costs that scale linearly with traffic.

evidence.excerpt: RAG systems introduce a recurring operational cost because each query retrieves external information and injects it into the model’s prompt. That additional context is billed on every request.
Per-query cost: the retrieval hop (~$0.0001) plus the LLM call ($0.005–$0.02). No GPU, no training, no ops. You can be in production in a week.
At a sustained scale, what appears flexible and inexpensive becomes a significant recurring expense.
RAG has lower upfront compute costs, but high query volumes quickly generate massive recurring token expenses due to large context windows.

qualifications: Recurring cost depends on retrieved token volume, reranking, caching, and vector-database pricing, all of which vary by design.

findings.statement: Sources disagree about where fine-tuning becomes cheaper than RAG: published crossover thresholds span roughly 100k queries per month to more than 100M, and one source asserts RAG is generally more cost-efficient, so no single crossover should be treated as settled.

evidence.excerpt: Below ~100k queries/month, the economics favour RAG.
evidence.context: Threshold stated from one vendor's production experience

evidence.excerpt: At very high traffic levels (100M+ queries per month), RAG’s per-request context overhead becomes significant.
evidence.context: Threshold from a modeled cost curve, three orders of magnitude above S-05

evidence.excerpt: RAG is generally more cost-efficient than fine-tuning because it limits resource costs by leveraging existing data and eliminating the need for extensive training stages.
evidence.context: Vendor FAQ asserting a general cost winner rather than a conditional crossover

evidence.excerpt: As shown in the earlier cost analysis, context expansion overhead grows with query volume, reaching approximately $43,750 per month at 50 million queries.
evidence.context: Illustrates the volume dependence that makes a single crossover claim fragile

qualifications: Each threshold is tied to a specific provider price list and assumed prompt length, so the disagreement may reflect assumptions as much as genuine disagreement.
S-05's figure is an operational rule of thumb; S-16's is a modeled break-even; S-19's is an unqualified preference.

findings.statement: Evaluation is layered: retrieval metrics (precision@k, recall@k, MRR, nDCG), generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, citation coverage, hallucination rate), and end-to-end checks for correctness, latency, cost, and safety.

evidence.excerpt: Core retrieval metrics include precision@k (are the top-k documents relevant?), recall@k (how much of the relevant info was retrieved?), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) (are correct docs ranked early?), and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG) (graded relevance with position weighting).

At the generation stage, the focus shifts to faithfulness (is output grounded in retrieved docs?), answer relevance (does it address the query?), citation coverage (are claims backed with sources?), and hallucination rate (unsupported or fabricated text).
Finally, evaluate the pipeline as users experience it: correctness vs factuality, latency and cost under load, and safety/compliance (refusal rates, harmful content, or policy violations).

Validate your retrieval accuracy (MRR, Context Recall) and generation quality (Faithfulness, Answer Relevance) using automated evaluation tools like Ragas or DeepEval before locking in infrastructure investments.

qualifications: Metric definitions are consistent across sources, but no source supplies enterprise-specific acceptance thresholds for an assistant, only examples such as a faithfulness floor above 0.85 (S-26).

findings.statement: Evaluation guidance in the corpus is RAG-centric; fine-tuning evaluation appears only as general guidance about task-specific metrics on held-out data, with no comparable benchmark set or acceptance thresholds for fine-tuned assistants.

evidence.excerpt: For fine-tuning, use task-specific metrics: accuracy and F1 for classification, BLEU or ROUGE for text generation. In both cases, evaluate on held-out data that reflects real usage, not just benchmarks.
Fine-tuned models can excel on fixed datasets, while RAG pipelines adapt to new knowledge but demand continuous monitoring and evaluation.
Fine tuned models should be re-evaluated quarterly at minimum against updated benchmark datasets to detect drift.

qualifications: This is a corpus gap rather than a claim that fine-tuning evaluation methods do not exist elsewhere.

findings.statement: Because RAG keeps sensitive content in an external store, sources say it supports retrieval-time access control, easier deletion, and source attribution, while fine-tuning embeds data in weights where granular access control and removal are difficult.

evidence.excerpt: RAG enforces document-level permissions directly during the vector retrieval stage using metadata filters. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge directly into neural network weights, making granular access control impossible without training separate models per authorization tier.
RAG’s approach keeps sensitive information within secured databases or knowledge repositories. The LLM only sees information at query time without storing it permanently in its weights.
keeping private data in a controlled retrieval layer allows organizations to update or restrict access without retraining

Adapted models synthesize answers from internal parameters, making it difficult to trace specific outputs back to particular source material—a significant governance limitation for regulated industries.
RAG also has the benefit that you can control who has access to which grounding data (based on who’s calling the model).

qualifications: The governance advantage assumes the retrieval layer itself is correctly access-controlled; S-24 and S-27 show that misconfigured retrieval is a primary failure mode.

findings.statement: RAG is not automatically more secure: it introduces indirect prompt injection, knowledge-base poisoning, and vector or embedding exposure, and the corpus documents reported incidents of each.

evidence.excerpt: Here, an attacker hides malicious instructions within an external document (e.g., a customer support ticket or an uploaded PDF). When the RAG system retrieves this poisoned document as context, the LLM unwittingly executes the hidden commands.
evidence.context: Security trade-press analysis of enterprise SaaS RAG incidents

evidence.excerpt: Unlike prompt injection, which targets execution logic, data poisoning targets the integrity of the knowledge base.
OWASP notes that files and websites can contain [indirect prompt injections](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) and that RAG does not fully remove that risk.
**Security and Compliance:** Since RAG often pulls from internal sources,**data security** and access control must be tightly managed.

qualifications: S-27 reports incidents with links to external sources that cannot be verified inside this corpus.
No source in the corpus offers a matching threat analysis for fine-tuned deployments, so the two sides are not symmetrically evidenced.

findings.statement: Access control must be enforced before retrieval: post-filtering a global top-k is unsafe and can leak through titles, snippets, counts, or timing, and the same rules must cover caches, summaries, logs, and citations.

evidence.excerpt: Push the allowed scope into both lexical and vector queries. Retrieving a global top-k and removing forbidden items afterward is unsafe and degrades recall: titles, snippets, counts, or timing can leak, while permitted passages may never enter the initial candidate set.
Access control is application logic, not a model instruction.
The most effective defense against data leakage is enforcing document-level permissions*during* the retrieval phase.
Search snippets, citations, result caches, conversation summaries, query logs, and offline evaluation copies must respect the same rules.

qualifications: S-24 is vendor material, but it explicitly separates its own model claims from proven capability and cites NIST ABAC and OWASP rather than its own benchmarks.

findings.statement: Hybrid architectures — fine-tune for behavior and format, retrieve for current facts — are widely recommended, but they inherit the complexity, cost, and skill requirements of both systems.

evidence.excerpt: The hybrid approach uses fine tuning for domain understanding and output structure while rag retrieval provides the latest facts and dynamic content.
A common and practical pattern is “fine-tune for format, RAG for knowledge.”
To sum up, you can freely combine the aforementioned methods at your convenience.
Using both approaches means inheriting the complexity of both systems.
Hybrid requires both ML and data engineering capabilities simultaneously, a combination few organizations have.

findings.statement: Sources citing retrieval-aware fine-tuning research (RAFT) claim that hybrids trained to reason over retrieved context outperform either approach alone, and warn that simply layering RAG on a fine-tuned model often fails.

evidence.excerpt: RAFT trains a model to operate in an “open-book” setting. It learns to process retrieved context, identify relevant passages, ignore distractors, and cite evidence accurately.
It is not enough to just combine RAG and fine-tuning. The model must be trained to reason over the retrieved context.

Yet research such as the [RAFT study](https://shishirpatil.github.io/publications/raft-2024.pdf) from UC Berkeley shows that hybrid systems combining retrieval and fine-tuning outperform either approach alone across benchmarks.
For example, using RAG to retrieve relevant information and then fine-tuning the model on that data (RAFT) can lead to more accurate and tailored outputs.

qualifications: The outperform claim is attributed to external benchmark papers; the corpus does not reproduce the experiments or the benchmark conditions.

findings.statement: Sources report that RAG dominates enterprise production adoption relative to fine-tuning, but the supporting numbers are survey-based or openly estimated rather than measured across a defined population.

evidence.excerpt: According to the [Menlo Ventures 2024](https://menlovc.com/2024-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/) State of Generative AI in the Enterprise report, 51 percent of enterprise AI deployments use RAG in production. Only nine percent rely primarily on fine-tuning.
Their adoption is widespread, with 86% of organizations augmenting LLMs using established RAG frameworks[4][5].
Currently, RAG is one of the most used methods in the domain of large language models; one can even assume that 90% of LLM-powered applications make use of RAG in one way or another.
evidence.context: The 90% figure is explicitly framed as an assumption by the author

qualifications: S-23's statistics are attributed to bracketed secondary citations without accessible methodology in the corpus.
Adoption share is not evidence of superiority; S-16 itself notes hybrid outperforms but adoption favors RAG because few teams have both skill sets.

findings.statement: The corpus contains no controlled head-to-head comparison of RAG and fine-tuning on the same enterprise task; comparative conclusions rest on vendor guidance, second-hand benchmark citations, and one independent RAG-only systems study, and sources explicitly caution against extrapolating benchmark results.

evidence.excerpt: Note that our study is not exhaustive.
evidence.context: The one independent research source limits its own scope

evidence.excerpt: The original [dense passage retrieval research](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.550/) illustrates why semantic representations can complement traditional sparse retrieval, but results from one public benchmark do not establish performance on a company's own content.
They do not prove retrieval recall, access isolation, groundedness, or production readiness.
No single method is universally superior to retrieval augmented generation for all enterprise ai use cases.
RAG is generally better for most enterprise use cases because it is more secure, scalable, and cost-efficient.
evidence.context: A vendor source that nonetheless asserts a general winner, illustrating the ranking claims the goal asks us to avoid adopting

findings.statement: Long context is presented as a complement to retrieval — used to reason over an already-narrowed, authorized evidence set — not as a replacement for retrieval over a changing corpus.

evidence.excerpt: Enterprise AI search is not a choice between RAG and a large context window.
Use RAG to narrow and locate evidence; use long context to reason over a larger but already authorized evidence set.
If you have only a small amount of data, then prompt engineering may suffice
evidence.context: Rising context windows expand what can be placed directly in the prompt for small or static datasets

qualifications: The long-context option is argued mostly by a single vendor source (S-24), which simultaneously states that its own model's specifications do not prove retrieval recall or production readiness.

findings.statement: Both approaches depend on data quality and continuous monitoring: irrelevant or stale documents degrade RAG, while mislabeled or biased training data degrade fine-tuned models, and both need drift detection.

evidence.excerpt: Poor data quality undermines both RAG and fine-tuning: irrelevant or outdated documents degrade RAG performance, while mislabeled or biased training data produces unreliable fine-tuned models.
Deficiencies at any stage compound into poor outputs at deployment.

Benchmark scores can highlight broad limitations, but governance and monitoring rely on RAG evaluation frameworks that support continuous evaluation, reproducibility, and integration with enterprise pipelines.
Continuously evaluate the pipeline using frameworks like RAGAS to detect if the knowledge base has been poisoned or if the model’s accuracy is decaying over time.

findings.statement: Sources converge on a small set of decision variables — how often knowledge changes, query volume, need for citations, output-format strictness, access-control needs, and team capability — even though the thresholds and weights attached to them differ.

evidence.excerpt: The question is no longer “Which approach is better?” It is “Under what conditions does each approach make economic and operational sense?”

Does the required knowledge change more than once a month? RAG. Do you need to cite sources to the user? RAG. Does the base model keep breaking an output schema a prompt can't fix? Fine-tune. Do you have >10,000 labelled examples of the behaviour you want? Fine-tune.
The rag vs fine tuning decision is rarely binary in production.
If the facts or data you rely on change daily or weekly (like stock prices, product catalogs, or regulations), RAG is usually the safer choice.

qualifications: The variables agree; the numeric triggers do not (see F-06), so the brief should present the variables as questions rather than as a scoring rubric.

findings.statement: Prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and distillation sit alongside RAG as ways to bring data to a model, and prompt engineering is the cheapest baseline for simple or small-data cases.

evidence.excerpt: The easiest way to facilitate interactions between a model and your data is to include the data in the instructions, or system prompt, sent to the model.
offers a simpler alternative for teams without external knowledge requirements, but lacks the depth of fine tuning or the currency of rag.
If you have only a small amount of data, then prompt engineering may suffice

qualifications: The goal scopes the decision to RAG, fine-tuning, and hybrid; prompt engineering is included only to prevent a false three-way binary.

gaps: No measured comparison of answer quality, hallucination rate, or task accuracy between RAG, fine-tuning, and hybrid on an identical enterprise assistant workload.
No published, reproducible evaluation protocol for fine-tuned assistants comparable to the RAG metric stack (precision@k, recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, citation coverage).
No agreed cost crossover point: thresholds in the corpus range from roughly 100k queries/month to more than 100M queries/month, with different underlying assumptions.
Little evidence on hybrid operational cost in practice, and none on the failure modes of hybrid orchestration beyond qualitative warnings about synchronization and routing complexity.

No corpus evidence on latency of a fine-tuned model versus RAG measured under the same traffic and hardware, so the latency comparison rests on architecture reasoning plus one RAG-only measurement study.
No treatment of fine-tuning-specific security threats (training-data extraction, memorization of PII) beyond brief mentions of leak risk and deletion difficulty.
No human-factors or team-skills data beyond assertions that hybrid requires both ML and data-engineering capabilities.

format.label: evidence-graded decision brief with a dimension-by-dimension trade-off comparison
format.why: The reader's task is a choice among three architectures judged against five named dimensions, so the document should be organized by those dimensions (freshness, evaluation, latency, cost, security) rather than as a narrative or a procedure. The corpus supplies comparative guidance, quantitative estimates, and one independent systems study — enough to compare dimensions and show where sources agree or conflict, but not enough for a ranked recommendation, a reproducible how-to, or a research paper with original results. An explicit evidence-strength section and per-dimension 'what this does not settle' notes let the brief respect the goal's instruction to preserve evidence limits and avoid unsupported rankings.
alternatives: A step-by-step implementation tutorial was rejected: the corpus contains architecture descriptions but no reproducible procedure with verified steps, and its numeric triggers conflict.

A literature review or research-paper structure was rejected: only one source is independent research (S-18) and it does not compare RAG with fine-tuning on a shared task, so there is no body of studies to review or methods to report.
A narrow cost-and-latency engineering deep dive was rejected as too narrow: it would discard the evaluation, security, and access-control evidence the goal explicitly asks about.
A pure vendor-comparison matrix was rejected because it would flatten genuine disagreements (for example the cost crossover in F-06) into a single grid.

outline.title: Reading this comparison: what the evidence can and cannot settle
outline.purpose: Set expectations before any recommendation: state that most sources are vendor guidance, that one independent study exists and is RAG-only, that adoption numbers are survey-based, and that the cost crossover is contested — so the reader knows no ranking follows.

outline.title: The core distinction: changing knowledge vs. changing behavior
outline.purpose: Give the reader the one framing that most sources share, so the five dimensions that follow have a consistent vocabulary; also note prompt engineering as the cheaper baseline that keeps the choice from looking falsely binary.

outline.title: Data freshness and knowledge updates
outline.purpose: Answer the first comparison dimension: where knowledge lives and how quickly it can change.

outline.title: RAG: freshness at query time
outline.purpose: Explain that retrieval decouples knowledge from weights, and note what that implies for update effort and citations.

outline.title: Fine-tuning: a knowledge snapshot baked into weights
outline.purpose: Explain the training-snapshot limitation and the retraining cycle it implies, without implying fine-tuning is unusable for stable domains.

outline.title: Long context is not a substitute for a changing corpus
outline.purpose: Close off a common false third option: large context windows help reason over an already-narrowed evidence set but do not solve currency or permission scoping.

outline.title: Latency and serving characteristics
outline.purpose: Present the retrieval-hop overhead with measured figures where they exist, and immediately flag that fine-tuned models are not guaranteed to be faster.

outline.title: Cost structure and the scale crossover
outline.purpose: Separate the two cost shapes (upfront training vs recurring retrieval) before addressing the disputed crossover point.

outline.title: RAG: low setup, recurring retrieval and context cost
outline.purpose: Show how retrieval cost grows linearly with traffic and which design choices change it.

outline.title: Fine-tuning: upfront training, cheaper inference
outline.purpose: Show where fine-tuning spend concentrates and why data preparation dominates it.

outline.title: Where the crossover is — and why the sources disagree
outline.purpose: Present the conflicting thresholds side by side and explain that the right comparison is the reader's own token volume and knowledge volatility, not a published number.

outline.title: Evaluation
outline.purpose: Give the team an evaluation plan per layer and be explicit that the corpus's fine-tuning evaluation material is thin.

outline.title: Measure retrieval, generation, and end-to-end separately
outline.purpose: List the concrete metric families and named tooling so the team can stand up a harness before choosing architecture.

outline.title: What is missing for fine-tuned assistants
outline.purpose: State plainly that fine-tuning evaluation guidance in the corpus is generic, so teams must define their own task metrics and acceptance thresholds.
outline.limitation: The corpus provides no benchmark set, metric definitions, or acceptance thresholds for evaluating a fine-tuned assistant comparable to the RAG metric stack; this section must present the absence rather than invent a protocol.

outline.title: Security, access control, and governance
outline.purpose: Frame security as a two-sided trade-off: retrieval keeps data external and governable but adds attack surface, while fine-tuning hides data in weights but makes control and deletion hard.

outline.title: Retrieval-time authorization and deletion
outline.purpose: Explain the mechanics of permission-aware retrieval and deletion across derived artifacts, including the failure mode of post-filtering a global top-k.

outline.title: RAG's own attack surface
outline.purpose: Counter the intuition that external storage is simply safer by describing indirect prompt injection, knowledge-base poisoning, and embedding exposure, with the incident evidence available.

outline.title: Hybrid approaches: what the evidence supports
outline.purpose: Explain the recommended hybrid pattern, what it requires to work (training the model to reason over retrieved context), and its honest cost and skill penalties.

outline.title: Keeping either approach healthy: data quality and monitoring
outline.purpose: Show that the choice does not remove the operational burden; both paths fail on data quality and need drift detection.

outline.title: Deciding for your team
outline.purpose: Convert the comparison into a set of questions the team can answer with its own numbers — volatility, volume, citation needs, format strictness, access-control scope, and available skills — without issuing a ranking.

outline.title: Open questions and evidence gaps
outline.purpose: List what the team would need to measure for itself, and name the corpus limits that prevent a stronger conclusion.
outline.limitation: No source provides a controlled head-to-head RAG-vs-fine-tuning comparison on a shared enterprise workload, so this section cannot cite a definitive study; it should state the gap and suggest the team's own benchmark instead.

diagrams.purpose: Show the division of labour in the hybrid pattern the corpus recommends, so readers can see which component owns behavior and which owns currency.
diagrams.caption: The hybrid pattern described in the corpus: a fine-tuned model owns behavior, tone, and output format, while a retrieval layer owns current, permission-filtered facts; the sources stress that the model must be trained to reason over retrieved context rather than having RAG simply layered on top [S-15][S-16].

diagrams.purpose: Make the ordering constraint visible: identity and policy evaluation happen before candidate generation, and every downstream artifact inherits the same permission scope.
diagrams.caption: The retrieval-time authorization sequence the corpus prescribes: the user's permitted scope is resolved and pushed into the lexical and vector queries before any candidates are generated, so forbidden documents never reach snippets, citations, or caches; retrieving a global top-k and filtering afterwards can still leak through counts, titles, or timing [S-24][S-27].

closing_rationale: A dimension-by-dimension decision brief fits because the corpus is comparative guidance rather than procedure or experiment: nineteen of the twenty sources are vendor or trade publications, and the single independent study characterizes RAG inference in isolation and states that its work 'is not exhaustive' [S-18]. Organizing by the goal's own axes lets each dimension be argued from the sources that actually address it — freshness from the Databricks, Monte Carlo, and IBM guides [S-15][S-19][S-08]; latency from the arXiv measurement study plus two vendor profiles [S-18][S-20][S-15]; cost from three sources whose thresholds disagree by three orders of magnitude [S-05][S-16][S-20]; evaluation from the one dedicated metrics article and the RAGAS-based builds [S-17][S-26]; and security from the threat reporting and access-control architecture pieces [S-27][S-24]. The brief also needs its evidence-frame and gaps sections because several sources do assert general winners — 'RAG is generally better for most enterprise use cases' [S-19] — and adopting those would violate the goal's instruction to avoid unsupported rankings; recording them as claims while presenting the disagreement openly is the honest alternative. The hybrid section is warranted rather than optional because the recommendation is near-unanimous [S-15][S-16][S-12], and the caution that hybrid inherits both systems' complexity [S-19] keeps it from becoming a fourth unsupported ranking.
